note: Hand-built ledger for a hand-authored chapter. Quotes are verbatim source text (MediaWiki markup kept); lines refer to the pinned raw files.

claims.statement: BIP39 was assigned in 2013 and its preamble records the status Deployed.

evidence.quote: Assigned: 2013-09-10
Status: Deployed

claims.statement: A mnemonic sentence is meant to be easier for people to handle than raw binary or hex: it can be written on paper or spoken over the telephone.

evidence.quote: A mnemonic code or sentence is superior for human interaction compared to the handling of raw binary or hexadecimal representations of a wallet seed.
The sentence could be written on paper or spoken over the telephone.

claims.statement: BIP39 transports computer-generated randomness; it is not a way to turn user-created sentences (brainwallets) into seeds.

evidence.quote: This guide is meant to be a way to transport computer-generated randomness with a human-readable transcription. It's not a way to process user-created sentences (also known as brainwallets) into a wallet seed.

claims.statement: BIP39 has two parts: generating the mnemonic and converting it into a binary seed.

evidence.quote: It consists of two parts: generating the mnemonic and converting it into a binary seed.

claims.statement: Entropy must be a multiple of 32 bits, between 128 and 256 bits.

evidence.quote: The mnemonic must encode entropy in a multiple of 32 bits.
The allowed size of ENT is 128-256 bits.

claims.statement: The checksum is the first ENT/32 bits of the SHA-256 hash of the entropy, appended to its end.

evidence.quote: A checksum is generated by taking the first ENT / 32 bits of its SHA256 hash. This checksum is appended to the end of the initial entropy.

claims.statement: The combined bits are split into 11-bit groups, each a number from 0 to 2047 used as an index into the wordlist.

evidence.quote: these concatenated bits are split into groups of 11 bits, each encoding a number from 0-2047, serving as an index into a wordlist.

claims.statement: CS = ENT/32 and MS = (ENT+CS)/11: 128 bits of entropy give 4 checksum bits and 12 words; 256 bits give 8 and 24.

evidence.quote: CS = ENT / 32 MS = (ENT + CS) / 11

claims.statement: Because the checksum is appended after the entropy, the final word mixes the last entropy bits with the checksum: 7 + 4 bits for 12 words, 3 + 8 bits for 24 words.

evidence.quote: This checksum is appended to the end of the initial entropy.

claims.statement: BIP39 describes an ideal wordlist: the first four letters identify a word, similar word pairs are avoided, and the list is sorted for efficient lookup.

evidence.quote: An ideal wordlist has the following characteristics:
it's enough to type the first four letters to unambiguously identify the word
word pairs like "build" and "built", "woman" and "women", or "quick" and "quickly"
the wordlist is sorted which allows for more efficient lookup of the code words

claims.statement: The pinned English wordlist has 2,048 sorted, unique entries whose first four letters are all distinct.

evidence.quote: [[bip-0039/bip-0039-wordlists.md|Wordlists]]

claims.statement: Wordlists with native characters must be encoded in UTF-8 using NFKD.

evidence.quote: The wordlist can contain native characters, but they must be encoded in UTF-8 using Normalization Form Compatibility Decomposition (NFKD).

claims.statement: Because most wallets support only English, BIP39 strongly discourages non-English wordlists for generating sentences.

evidence.quote: Since the vast majority of BIP39 wallets supports only the English wordlist, it is '''strongly discouraged''' to use non-English wordlists for generating the mnemonic sentences.

claims.statement: BIP39 lists its short checksum as a shortcoming: modest odds of catching random errors (it cites 1 in 256 missed) and no help correcting them.

evidence.quote: The checksum is short. This means it only gives modest odds of catching random errors (1-in-256 errors will be missed). It is also not able to provide any assistance in correcting errors.

claims.statement: With 4 checksum bits, 128 of the 2,048 possible final words give a valid 12-word sentence (1 in 16); with 8 bits, 8 of 2,048 give a valid 24-word sentence (1 in 256).

evidence.quote: CS = ENT / 32
1-in-256 errors will be missed

claims.statement: Using a sentence not generated by BIP39's algorithm is possible but not advised, and software must compute its checksum and warn if it is invalid.

evidence.quote: Although using a mnemonic not generated by the algorithm described in "Generating the mnemonic" section is possible, this is not advised and software must compute a checksum for the mnemonic sentence using a wordlist and issue a warning if it is invalid.

claims.statement: The seed is PBKDF2 with the NFKD sentence as password, "mnemonic" + passphrase (NFKD) as salt, 2048 iterations of HMAC-SHA512, and a 64-byte output.

evidence.quote: we use the PBKDF2 function with a mnemonic sentence (in UTF-8 NFKD) used as the password and the string "mnemonic" + passphrase (again in UTF-8 NFKD) used as the salt. The iteration count is set to 2048 and HMAC-SHA512 is used as the pseudo-random function. The length of the derived key is 512 bits (= 64 bytes).

claims.statement: The passphrase is optional; when absent, the empty string is used.

evidence.quote: If a passphrase is not present, an empty string "" is used instead.

claims.statement: Seed generation uses the sentence and is completely independent from how the sentence was generated.

evidence.quote: The conversion of the mnemonic sentence to a binary seed is completely independent from generating the sentence.

claims.statement: Every passphrase generates a valid seed and wallet; only the correct one opens the intended wallet. BIP39 calls this plausible deniability.

evidence.quote: every passphrase generates a valid seed (and thus a deterministic wallet) but only the correct one will make the desired wallet available.

claims.statement: Unlike an application's unlock password, a wrong BIP39 passphrase does not fail: it silently leads to a different wallet.

evidence.quote: every passphrase generates a valid seed (and thus a deterministic wallet) but only the correct one will make the desired wallet available.

claims.statement: Because the seed is computed from the words, the same entropy written with another wordlist gives a different seed, and a seed cannot be turned back into a sentence.

evidence.quote: translating the mnemonic to a different wordlist necessarily creates a completely different seed.
the conversion is one-way only (from BIP-0039 sentence to BIP-0032 seed).

claims.statement: The seed can then be used to generate deterministic wallets using BIP32 or similar methods.

evidence.quote: This seed can be later used to generate deterministic wallets using BIP-0032 or similar methods.

claims.statement: BIP39's test vectors live in trezor/python-mnemonic and use the passphrase TREZOR; separate Japanese vectors exercise heavily normalized passphrases.

evidence.quote: The passphrase "TREZOR" is used for all vectors.
https://github.com/trezor/python-mnemonic/blob/master/vectors.json
(Japanese wordlist test with heavily normalized symbols as passphrase)

claims.statement: NFKD expands the single character ㍍ into the four characters メートル; all 24 Japanese vectors depend on this kind of normalization.

evidence.quote: (Japanese wordlist test with heavily normalized symbols as passphrase)
(again in UTF-8 NFKD)

claims.statement: BIP39 lists the lack of a versioning scheme among its shortcomings, noting it is now largely mitigated by descriptor wallets; its authors proposed SLIP-0039 as an intended successor.

evidence.quote: No versioning scheme. When originally introduced, there was no way to distinguish the address format that should be used for a BIP-0039 key. This is now largely mitigated by use of descriptor wallets (BIP-0380) in addition to a seed however.
The authors of BIP-0039 proposed the [https://github.com/satoshilabs/slips/blob/master/slip-0039.md SLIP-0039] scheme as an intended successor to BIP-0039 improving on the above shortcomings.

claims.statement: The seed step places no constraints on sentence structure; clients may use their own wordlists or sentence generators.

evidence.quote: there are no constraints on sentence structure and clients are free to implement their own wordlists or even whole sentence generators
is possible, this is not advised

claims.statement: For the published all-zero 128-bit vector, the 4 checksum bits are 0011, so eleven groups are index 0 (abandon) and the last is index 3 (about).

evidence.quote: The test vectors include input entropy, mnemonic and seed.
